## Appendix A: Welfare summary items (for the PI)

**The welfare-critical list is not widened, and no limit is softened.** Task 20 compares every listed function, module
and line with `d3a1070`, byte for byte: `bounds.py`, `welfare.py`, `marks.py` and `stranded.py` whole;
`preflight.gate` and `out_of_cage`; the listed `Service` functions, `_start` among them; `Session._ends`, `_hold`,
`_manual_reward`, `set`, `_schedule` and `OUTSIDE_A_RUN`; `link._setting`; `cli._settle_departure`, `_settle_return`
and `main`'s `_marks.depart(session, departure)` line: each the same. `Session._command` changes by exactly the four
insertions below and nothing else, and with them taken out equals the base.

**Approved for the design on 2026-10-30, "Approve all four"**, quoted from the spec's §14 as they were put to him; the
final code returns to him with the plan:

1. **`Session._command` gains three branches beside the pause** (hand back, range, revert), each handing to a
   function off the list, as C2a's and C2b's buttons did; its listed `held` pass-through and `except` line are
   unchanged.
2. **One line in `Session._command`'s setting path, ahead of `set`**, runs §9's live refusal, so the listed `except`
   line turns an impossible change into a refusal on the feed; the listed parts are unchanged.
3. **Revert goes on the welfare summary** (engine spec §20 item 3): it restores task settings and drawn ranges only,
   never a bounded setting such as a reward size (§17.6); each value goes through `Session.set` unchanged, and the
   revert is refused whole if any value is.
4. **Unchanged byte for byte: `Session.set`, `link._setting`, `Service._start` and `stranded.py`.** `Session.set`
   stays so because change ids are assigned where changes apply (`_apply_staged`, off the list), and the live layer
   stays merged in the run's values, its names kept apart and recorded beside them. The welfare comparison at merge,
   function by function on exact source, shows it.

As built: items 1 and 2 are the diff Task 20 prints (Tasks 12, 13 and 14 make it); each new function turns any fault
of its own into a refusal, so a button never ends the session (Call 20), and a fault in the live check refuses the
edit, never the session (Call 26). Item 3 is Task 14's; item 4, Tasks 7 and 20's: the resume reader learns every new
kind of change row in the commit that first writes one, still refusing a damaged row, and a reward size is still
restored only from ordinary setting rows.

**An amendment to item 3, approved by the PI on 2026-10-31** (the outline review's I-9; worded from Tasks 13 and 14 as built):

5. ***Hand back* and *change a range* do not pass through the checked setting path (`Session.set`), whether pressed
   as buttons or made by a revert, and neither can touch a reward.** Item 3 says each value a revert puts back goes
   through `Session.set`; its values still do, but its hand-backs and ranges go the way the buttons do. What bounds
   them instead:
   - **A hand-back carries no new value**: it puts back the run's own starting value, the task's start under the
     run's. That value was judged at the run's start for trials no animal can get right (the pre-flight, and
     `Session.run` behind it), and a `wlx taskd` run's pre-flight range-checked it; values given by `wlx run --set` are
     not range-checked (XC-371). When it is offered, the hand-back is judged again for trials no animal can get right,
     and **where that value lies outside its declared range it is checked again as a typed value outside its range
     is**, with the widened load checks over the ranges in force now, and refused at once if that refuses it: a range
     widened since the run started could otherwise meet a run value no check had judged with it (the plan's
     engineering review, I-3, which found that gap and is fixed here).
   - **A range is a draw's numbers, never one value.** Each number is a finite number from the wire's own checker
     (`link._setting`, unchanged); the range must be one that can be drawn; it must leave no trial no animal can get
     right; and each end past the setting's declared range is checked as a typed value outside its range is, with the
     widened load checks. Only the draw the open block uses can change, on a setting that may change live: never a
     weighted set, a list, a direction or a condition's own range.
   - **Inside a revert**, its hand-backs and ranges are judged for trials no animal can get right; neither is checked
     again as a typed value, since a revert puts back a moment the run held, every act that made that moment checked
     as it applied (a value and a range widened over the whole plan, a hand-back now too).
   - **Every such change is also judged against the trials waiting to be shown again**, with the values they keep
     (Call 42), so a drummed trial cannot come back impossible.
   - **A reward size cannot be reached**: it is never a task setting, a draw naming one is refused at load, and both
     acts refuse a reward size's name by name.

   *Recommended: approve.* **The PI, 2026-10-31: "Approve (Recommended)".** (Tasks 13, 14)

**For information:**

6. **A drawn or live-changed wait can be longer than the task declares**, under your approved `longer-than-declared`
   warning (2026-10-12, "Allow, with a warning"). It happens only where the task declares a draw past its range (the
   pre-flight warns) or a person widens a range live (warned as a typed value is). While a trial waits through it,
   stop, pause and the out-of-cage limit are heard only when that trial ends (XC-373), and the five-minute trial cap
   still ends it.
7. **The three combinations XC-343 names are refused in the file, at a run's start and live** (your Q10; review I-5),
   so drumming cannot bring an impossible trial back forever, holding a time limit open. **Live, a change is also
   judged against the trials waiting to come back with the values they keep**: the plan's session fuzz found a
   drummed trial keeping a response deadline from before a live change, under a target hold set in the same moment,
   which in its reduction came back 18,531 times until the out-of-cage limit ended the session; that change is now
   refused at once with the sentence naming the condition (Call 42, Task 13; the alternative is Appendix B item 16).
8. **The function that applies changes at the trial boundary is rewritten** (`_apply_staged`, off the list) to write
   the change log. Its reward-size branch stays `bounds.set`, in the same pass as its strobe and its row, and the
   existing tests that pin that are kept unedited. (Task 7)

## Appendix B: For the PI to confirm

**Answered 2026-10-31** (`answers.md`, "Plan approval round", asked in the UI): items 2 to 9 and 11 to 16, "Confirm
all as built (Recommended)"; items 1, 10, 17 and 18 as each says below, each built in revision round 2 (Call 45).

1. **A sequence-balanced block's cycle shows every pair once: the linear de Bruijn sequence.** **The PI, 2026-10-31:
   "Add one closing trial (Recommended)"** ("17 a cycle, every pair once (aguirre2007)"). **Built so:** each cycle
   plays the linear de Bruijn sequence of its conditions at its depth, n^depth + depth − 1 trials (17 for 4
   conditions at pairs, 66 at triples), so every pair (every triple) is shown once per cycle. The first depth − 1
   trials of each cycle are a lead-in that only precedes what follows, and each such trial's line marks it
   (`planned`'s `lead_in`) so an analysis can drop it; wl-preproc is told the key before it is written (Task 3). A
   condition's target stays the places it plays past the lead-ins; the block owes its plan's places, the lead-in's
   among them (item 11). The cost: the lead-in's conditions are shown once more per cycle. Published serially
   balanced designs work this way (Aguirre 2007, whose abstract recommends them; that their length is n² + 1 is
   UNVERIFIED, the full text not read). It was built first at the spec's n² trials, which showed 15 of 16 pairs in
   the last cycle.
2. **Where it cannot be read whether a live change made a trial easier, the trial does not count toward moving up.**
   That happens only where a setting is read against the trial's background (a luminance, say), against another
   setting that holds no number, or against nothing. A changed choice, or a changed appearance, is read by what its
   declared meaning says changing it does. *Recommended: never move an animal up on doubt.*
3. **Changing a drawn range live changes the draw the current block uses, for the rest of the run.** If that is the
   task's draw, every block using it gets the new range; if the block has its own draw, only that block type. Only
   numbers change: a uniform's ends, a normal's numbers, a wait's shortest, average and longest. These are not changed
   live in C3, each filed for later:
   - a weighted set or a prepared list;
   - a direction's range;
   - a setting declared not live.

   *Recommended.*
4. ***Hand back* gives back a value a person set; it does not undo a changed range.** A range is put back by typing its
   numbers again, or by revert. *Recommended.*
5. **Revert reaches back within the current run**: to any change made in it, or to the run's start. *Recommended:
   between runs each run starts fresh anyway.*
6. **A priming block's runs count only trials whose stimulus appeared.** A priming block ends on its number of trials
   or its time limit (one is required), and its conditions owe no fixed number of trials. A break in it writes no
   shortfall. *Recommended.*
7. **Each time a sequence-balanced block type opens, it plays a new sequence drawn from the run's seed**, including
   after *back one*. *Recommended: replayable from the seed.*
8. **A range of directions that crosses rightward is written 315° to 45°.** The task writes it its own way, e.g. −45°
   to 45°; the record, the change log and the console show what the rig draws from 0° up to 360°. A direction you or
   the task give is written as given, with the load warning you chose. *For your information (the controller's
   ruling).*
9. **A trial brought back "again at once" is moved past after the task's repeat limit, as any repeat is** (review I-4).
   Without this, a trial the animal always breaks would come back forever, holding the block open. Past the limit it is
   recorded as moved past, flagged as possible avoidance as today, and the sequence goes on. *Recommended.*
10. **In a training progression, eased trials do not count toward a stage's end by its number of trials or its
    targets** (review I-7). Your rule is that an animal is never moved up on eased trials. A stage with no criterion
    ends when its trials are run or its targets met, so counting eased trials there would move the animal up on them.
    They still count toward moving back and in the condition's own counts on the record. **A sequence-balanced stage
    below the top** ends when its planned sequence is played out, eased trials included, and then the animal moves up.
    **The PI, 2026-10-31: "Only warn at load"** ("the stage moves up as usual; the task file gets a load warning").
    **Built so:** the stage moves up when its sequence is played out, eased trials or not, as before, and the load
    warns of such a stage, `sequence-stage-moves-up`: "it moves up when its sequence is played out, eased trials or
    not" (Task 5; in the warnings list and the engine spec's §19).
11. **A sequence-balanced block owes the places of its plan it has not played** (and one more for a trial waiting to
    come back at once), **and nothing once its number of trials or a time limit cuts it short.** The places it never
    reached stay listed in its planned sequence on the record, with no shortfall for them. Its plan's places include
    each cycle's lead-in (item 1), so a lead-in's condition owes one more a cycle than its target. *Confirmed as
    built.*
12. **In a designed block, *clear* moves past only a trial waiting to come back** (a drummed one, or one due again at
    once), one trial; clearing anything else there is refused with a sentence, since the plan would play that place
    anyway. *Recommended.*
13. **A time limit does not wait for a trial due "again at once"**; only a drummed trial holds it, as your "Finish the
    drum first" says. The waiting trial is dropped, as a waiting repeat is. *Recommended.*
14. **In a priming block run by a chance, a run's recorded length is the trials it showed**; no length is planned
    until the chance switches. Under drawn run lengths it is the drawn length. *Recommended.*
15. **Revert on the page asks for no confirmation**, but each moment now says beneath it what a revert to it would
    change, setting by setting, before you press it (the science review's M-1). It is guarded against a double click,
    and a revert can itself be reverted. *Recommended.*
16. **A live change that would leave a trial waiting to come back impossible is refused at once** (your Q10, "Refuse
    in file and live"; Appendix A item 7). A repeat keeps the value its trial drew for a setting declared `same`, even
    after the range it came from changed, so the change is judged against what the waiting trials keep. *For your
    information, with the option:* the alternative is to draw a `same` value fresh where keeping it would make the
    trial impossible, which would accept the change and break "same" for that trial. The refusal now ends with the
    way on: "clear the waiting trial, switch drumming off or pause, then make the change" (the science review's M-3).
17. **Cued designs and the two look checks** (your Q10, "Refuse in file and live"; the science review's C-1). A task
    is refused when its target can look like its distractors, or when two objects swap looks from trial to trial.
    That is right for a pop-out search, where the target is the odd one out, but not for a cued design: a cue or a
    remembered sample says which of two identical-looking objects is the target (the classic cued two-choice task,
    Chelazzi et al. 1993), or a cue says which of several identical placeholders to look at. **The PI, 2026-10-31:
    "Refuse only odd-one-out tasks (Recommended)"** ("refuse only where the task declares its target is found by its
    look; warn otherwise (chelazzi1993)"). **Built so:** an array gains one word, `found_by`, `"look"` by default (the
    odd one out) or `"cue"` (a cue, a remembered sample or a place names the target), any other word refused at load.
    The two look checks refuse only where the target is found by its look, and a swap where any array in it is;
    where a cue names it they are a load warning, `cued-target`: "the target must be named by a cue; check that one is
    shown", the same at a run's start; live, a change they would refuse on an odd-one-out array is accepted on a cued
    one, with no warning carried back, since the live check has no path that carries one (the load and the start said
    it; Call 45). The no-time-to-answer refusal stays whatever names the target. It was built first refusing every
    case.
18. **A drawn range changed live, and moving up** (your Q8, "eased trials do not count toward moving up"; the science
    review's I-2). **The PI, 2026-10-31: "Judge the range as a whole (Recommended)"** ("if the new range reaches
    anything easier than the written one, none of its trials count toward moving up"). **Built so:** when a person
    changes a drawn range live, the new range is judged as a whole against the written one: if it reaches any value
    easier than the written range allows (for a uniform, either end moved the easier way; anything that cannot be
    read, or mixed, counts as easier, as doubt does under item 2), none of its trials count toward moving up until
    the range is put back, by typing the written numbers again or by revert. A normal's mean and cut, and a wait's
    shortest, average and longest, are read as a uniform's ends are; a normal's spread changed counts as mixed. The
    change's row in the change log says which way it went. The trial-by-trial comparison it was built with first
    (each trial against what the written range would have drawn at the same random point) is removed; a value a
    person holds is still judged against what the trial would otherwise have had.
